author: fwyzard
body: #### PR description: Every module call copies the job's `ServiceToken` (a `std::shared_ptr`), or locks a `ServiceWeakToken` to it, and then releases it. This happens in `Path::runNextWorkerAsync`/`workerFinished`, in the worker tasks and in every `ServiceRegistry::Operate`. All threads of the job therefore update the same atomic reference count. On a large machine this cache line bounces between cores and sockets, and it becomes the bottleneck of the whole job. This PR adds `ServiceRegistry::OperateNonOwning`. It makes the services available on the current thread through a non-owning pointer, saving and restoring the previous context by move, without touching the reference count. `presentToken()` still returns an owning token, and asserts that it never hands out the non-owning one. All asynchronous framework tasks now receive the caller's token by reference, and store a pointer to it when they need it later, instead of a copy or a `ServiceWeakToken`; they use `OperateNonOwning` to make the services available: - the event path: `EventProcessor::processEventAsyncImpl`, `StreamSchedule` per-event tasks, `Path`, worker prefetch, acquire and run tasks, pre-prefetch selection; - transforms, workers without prefetching, stream and global transitions (`StreamSchedule`, `GlobalSchedule`); - the module-facing transform interface: `doTransformAsync` / `transformAsync_` in the `global`, `limited`, `one` and `stream` module base classes and their `implementors.h` now take a `ServiceToken const&` instead of a `ServiceWeakToken const&`; - the delayed reader (`DelayedReaderInputProductResolver`), EventSetup callbacks (`CallbackBase`, `CallbackExternalWork`, `ESProductResolverTemplate`), `SourceCoordinator`, and the run and lumi transitions in `EventProcessor`. This relies on the caller keeping the token alive until the asynchronous work it starts has finished. Before, a task that outlived its token would get an empty token from `ServiceWeakToken::lock()`; now it would use a dangling pointer. The condition already holds for the `EventProcessor`'s token, for `TestProcessor`, and for `SecondaryEventProvider`, which waits with `syncWait`. The once-per-job code (construction, `beginJob`/`endJob`, `writeProcessBlock`) still uses owning tokens. An alternative approach, with one independent token (control block) per stream, gives the same throughput. It was not used because it only spreads the contention instead of removing it. ##### Measurements - **Hardware:** 2 AMD EPYC 9655 (96 cores per socket, SMT 2, 380 usable hardware threads in the container), CPU only. - **Software and input:** `CMSSW_20_1_X_2026-10-11-1300`, the full HLT menu `/online/collisions/2026/2e34/v1.3/HLT/V2` running on CPUs only, on run 402360 HLTPhysics data. The input is read with `DAQSource` (`FRDPreUnpack`) from local FRD files. - **Job setup:** each job runs alone on the node, pinned with `taskset` to N physical cores and both of their SMT siblings, with threads = streams = 2N. - **Throughput:** measured by the `ThroughputService`, skipping the first 300 and the last 100 events. Job sizes go from 10400 to 49800 events, so that each measurement lasts at least 60 s. - **Clock normalisation:** the cpu clock of the job's cores is sampled every second from `/proc/cpuinfo`. The plots show the throughput normalised to a constant 3.2 GHz clock (throughput 3.2 GHz / mean measured clock), to separate scaling from frequency changes. - **Scan 1:** fill socket 0 first (1 to 95 cores), then add cores on socket 1 (up to 190 cores). - **Scan 2:** use n cores on each socket, for n = 1 to 95. The measurements were done with the first two commits of this PR, before the `presentToken()` check and the changes to the transform interface and to the EventSetup callback tasks; measurements with the final version are in progress. | cores | before (ev/s) | after (ev/s) | after / before | |---|---|---|---| | 95, one socket | 380 (377 at 3.2 GHz) | 422 (445 at 3.2 GHz) | 1.11 (1.18 at 3.2 GHz) | | 96, 48 on each socket | 431 (343 at 3.2 GHz) | 505 (418 at 3.2 GHz) | 1.17 (1.22 at 3.2 GHz) | | 190, both sockets | 448 (382 at 3.2 GHz) | 763 (820 at 3.2 GHz) | 1.70 (2.15 at 3.2 GHz) | Mean of two repetitions of each scan; the spread between the repetitions is below 1% for all points except the PR at 190 cores in scan 1 (1.4%). The 95-core and 190-core rows are from scan 1, the 96-core row is from scan 2. Up to about 48 cores the throughput with and without this PR differs by less than 3%. Without this PR, throughput stops increasing at about 450 ev/s once more than about 110 cores are used, wherever they are. With this PR it scales almost linearly up to the full machine: at a fixed clock, 190 cores reach 86-89% of linear scaling from the first point (scan 1 and scan 2). The profile of a 190-core job confirms the cause: before this PR the IPC was 0.73, and with the event-path part of the change (first commit) it is about 1.56, with the same number of instructions per event. The remaining `shared_ptr` reference counting takes less than 0.5% of the cycles. The `FastTimerService` time not accounted to modules ("other") drops from about 485 to about 36 ms per event, and the total real time per event from about 860 to about 515 ms. #### PR validation: - New unit tests in `FWCore/ServiceRegistry` cover `OperateNonOwning` nested with `Operate` in both orders, and check that `presentToken()` returns an owning token while the services are made available by `OperateNonOwning`. - All unit tests in `FWCore/Framework`, `FWCore/ServiceRegistry`, `FWCore/TestProcessor` and `FWCore/Integration` pass (190/190), with all of CMSSW rebuilt. - The full Run 3 HLT menu ran on 1 to 190 cores without errors.
title: Improve framework scalability above 100 cores
